source.title: "Do Not Rely on the Linear Representation Hypothesis" (blog post)
source.citation: "Do Not Rely on the Linear Representa…

record.tranche_reason: The post reports experiments that challenge or qualify the general linear-representation premise, but they do not test the specified superposition, capacity, polysemantic-neuron, SAE, or feature-dimensionality versions.
record.gate_note: The reported steering efficacy and crosstalk results are included. Learned coefficients, vector norms, and steering layers are not rows because they are optimization or intervention details rather than outcomes. The response examples are illustrative, not separately measured results.
record.test_reason: The post optimizes steering vectors by gradient descent so that one direction steers four tasks at four norms, and two vectors sum to an unrelated task. This targets two linear-representation tenets: intensity as scaling and composition as addition. It does not measure superposition in toy models, neuron polysemanticity, capacity allocation, SAE feature recovery or stability, or feature dimensionality. The vectors are built on purpose to show the effect rather than found in the model's own representations. The record's 'tests/T5' contradicts its own tranche_reason, which says no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. To add: the author argues practitioners should treat linearity as a hypothesis to test, not a premise. He also contends that gradient-optimized vectors are no less 'natural' than difference-of-means or SAE vectors. He concedes the results do not rule out that some directions are truly linear (the weak LRH).
record.recipe_differences: The study optimizes activation-steering vectors by gradient descent on task likelihood with KL regularization, rather than testing the toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The four-task steering experiment reports higher aggregate efficacy for larger Qwen3 models, with crosstalk remaining similar. The tested layer is described as 40% through the network; the appendix lists different layer indices for models.

fits_no_version.finding: A single gradient-optimized direction steers Qwen3 models to four different tasks at four learned norms. Qwen3-14B mean efficacy is +0.76 with crosstalk +0.04, and efficacy rises with model size (+0.29 at 1.7B to +0.76 at 14B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLMs, changing only the magnitude of a steering direction can change which behaviour it elicits, contrary to 'intensity as scaling'.

fits_no_version.finding: Vectors optimized to steer for French and for negative sentiment sum to a vector that steers for code style. Code-style efficacy runs from +0.45 (1.7B) to +0.92 (14B), with low reported crosstalk.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLMs, adding two steering vectors need not compose their behaviours; the sum can elicit an unrelated behaviour, contrary to 'composition as addition'.

record.problems: The reported experiments use optimized steering vectors and therefore do not establish that naturally learned features or neuron representations have the same properties. The results concern Qwen3 models and task-steering scores, not feature geometry. The text reports no uncertainty estimates or control-vector comparison, and refers readers elsewhere for detailed evaluation and dataset-generation procedures.
record.rows_left_out: No reported outcome rows were omitted. Appendix values for learned scales, vector norms, cosine similarity, and selected layers were not outcomes of the claim-relevant task evaluations.

untested.parts: Entire version: no toy models, sparsity sweep, feature overlap or geometry.
Entire version: no neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity allocation.
Entire version: neurons are not examined.
Entire version: no measure of features spread across neurons, and no SAE recovery.
Entire version: SAE features are only mentioned in the naturalness argument; none are trained or evaluated.
Entire version: the dimensionality of naturally learned features is not measured. The optimized vectors show nonlinear responses to engineered directions, not the shape of the model's features.

record.verdict_notes: The study bears on the linear representation hypothesis, which superposition accounts presuppose, but none of the stated versions. Its counterexamples are deliberately optimized interventions; no uncertainty or control-vector comparisons are reported. The appendix values (alphas, norms, cosine around -0.13 to -0.21) are correctly excluded as rows. The post is unreviewed; it is dated 2026 and cites 2026 works.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, sparse-feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether neuron polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure; the study manipulates steering vectors, not neurons or their feature content.
Whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or are sparse features recoverable by a dictionary or SAE.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional; steering-vector behavior is not a test of feature dimensionality.
